abstract: Genomic prediction models for polyploid crops often partition genetic variance into additive and dominance-labelled components, but a fitted dominance component is not necessarily identifiable as digenic dominance (D2). We combined known-truth simulations with a panel-conditioned diagnostic workflow on 11 public datasets from alfalfa, potato, blueberry, guinea grass, rose, Miscanthus, sweetpotato and sugarcane. The workflow uses kernel geometry, permutation references, structure controls, planted-D2 spike-ins, posterior uncertainty and paired prediction tests. In autotetraploid simulations, the standard additive-plus-dominance model assigned appreciable variance to the dominance kernel when true D2 was absent, and its share responded only weakly to planted D2 signal. In crop panels, additive and dominance kernels were highly collinear, and Bayesian degree-kernel decompositions did not localize non-additive variance to D2, although restricted maximum likelihood placed it on D2 in alfalfa and potato. Observed shares exceeded matched permutation references by more than the pre-set margin in two of nine autotetraploid datasets, and no dataset met the criteria for biological D2 interpretation. A large fitted share was not sufficient for cross-validated prediction gain. We recommend reporting these components with diagnostics that separate biologically supported dominance, prediction-useful kernels and unresolved model-basis contributions.
